items.recapEn: At the old tororo teahouse in Mariko, Ken ate two bowls of grated yam over barley rice and decided to learn the recipe; the cook, Aoki-san, let him into the kitchen. Hana listed what she can do now since Nihonbashi and decided she walks for the diary. That night Ken wrote the recipe on its last page, unasked.

items.recapEn: In the kitchen doorway Hana asked Ken whether he had really decided to learn tororo-jiru. Yes: so that he can make it someday at his own place, a counter-only shop serving one dish a day, all learned on the road. He asked to borrow her diary; she refused. Aoki-san scolded him, and Ken said hai for the first time.

items.recapEn: The menu card of the Mariko tororo teahouse: the tororo-jiru set with barley rice and tea for 1,600 yen, a children's set for 800, a free second bowl of rice. It explains how to eat it: rice in the bowl, tororo poured over, mixed with chopsticks, eaten almost like a drink. Closed Thursdays; the recipe is four hundred years old.
